paragraphs: The opening page makes Lin's hesitation visible through objects. On Sunday evening he is smiling at his phone beside books, a mug and the long trailing pothos, joking, "My pothos looks like noodles. Now THAT'S a story." The group chat is asking for a fun Friday lunch story, so he clearly has something he wants to share. Then the test sheet appears with INTROVERT in large type and "Not good at public speaking" highlighted. By the next panel, the metaphor has become physical: Lin is crouched inside a cardboard box marked INTROVERT, saying, "Better not. My type won't allow it." The joke works because the label has shifted from a description on paper into a container he is treating as a rule.

Cilantro provides the comic turning point. At lunch, the cook cheerfully raises a large bunch and announces, "Double cilantro for you!" Lin reacts instantly: "Wait! I have a few things to say!" Three minutes later he is gesturing energetically over the noodles and explaining, "Add that, and the whole bowl belongs to the cilantro!" while the cook answers, "Got it. Not a leaf." Yuan is laughing beside him. The scene does not prove that Lin is secretly some other personality type, and it does not erase his nervousness. It simply gives him a funny piece of evidence that his willingness to speak changes with the subject, the situation and how much he cares about what is being discussed.

The lower page keeps that discovery modest. After lunch, Yuan points back to the contradiction with, "Why didn't your type stop you just now?" Lin replies, "Maybe it hates cilantro too," keeping the joke on the situation rather than turning it into a personality verdict. Walking back to work, he admits, "I'll still get nervous up there." Yuan does not tell him to become outgoing; she suggests a smaller task: "Pick a familiar topic. Just three minutes." That evening, the cardboard box is still in the room, but Lin is now preparing instead of hiding. His line, "Three photos beat a cardboard box," sits beside a notebook listing how he nearly killed the plant, kept it alive, and is still not giving up.

Friday's presentation deliberately shows that progress and discomfort can coexist. Lin stands in front of coworkers with a pothos photo behind him and begins, "Hi, everyone. I..." A small narration box says, "Still nervous. Still here." The next panel is labeled "Three minutes," and the visual payoff returns to the noodle joke: "I tried to grow a forest. I got a bowl of noodles." Someone in the audience asks, "Did it survive?" and Lin answers, "Still trying. Just like me." He has not transformed into a fearless speaker. What has changed is narrower and more believable: he prepared something familiar, stayed through the awkward opening, found a joke that belonged to his real experience, and completed the short share.

The ending does not ask Lin to abandon quietness. Back home, he sits with tea while a cat sleeps by the window, plants fill the room, and he says, "Enough talking for today. A quiet evening tomorrow." The word INTROVERT is now kept in his notebook rather than worn as the front of a box, while the cardboard box has returned to being an ordinary object beside the pothos. The banner says, "Labels are notes, not seals," and the closing line adds, "Names can help. They don't have to write your life." Read alongside the supplied Chapter 32 excerpt, the comic is a contemporary reflection rather than a literal translation: names can help us notice and organize experience, while "knowing when to stop" can also mean noticing the point where a useful name starts becoming a boundary that experience itself does not support.
a-label-is-not-a-whole-person.title: A Label Can Describe You Without Deciding You
a-label-is-not-a-whole-person.teaser: Lin is ready to tell the office about his pothos, which has grown so stringy that it looks like noodles. Then a personality test calls him an INTROVERT and says he is not good at public speaking, so he literally climbs into a cardboard box. The surprise is that cilantro gets him talking, Yuan notices, and a three-minute plant story becomes a small experiment in letting experience add detail to a label.
a-label-is-not-a-whole-person.quote: As things are first defined, names arise. Once names exist, one must also know where to stop. Knowing where to stop is how one avoids danger.
a-label-is-not-a-whole-person.practice: Think of one small thing you have postponed because you told yourself, "I'm just not that kind of person." Try a version small enough to give you new information rather than a new identity: choose a familiar topic, give yourself three minutes, or tell one trusted person. Afterwards, write down what actually happened, including both the awkward parts and the easier ones, without rushing to replace the old label with a new one.
a-label-is-not-a-whole-person.comicTitle: Found Your Type? Don't Box Yourself In
a-label-is-not-a-whole-person.comicAlt: A two-page Art Nouveau comic follows Lin, a bespectacled man surrounded by pothos plants, from wanting to share a funny plant story to hiding inside a cardboard box labeled INTROVERT after reading a personality test. A cilantro-heavy lunch unexpectedly gets him talking, Yuan encourages him to try a familiar three-minute topic, and he later gives a nervous but funny office presentation about his noodle-like pothos. The story ends at home with tea, a sleeping cat, the INTROVERT label stored in his notebook, and the message, "Labels are notes, not seals."

listen-before-giving-expertise.title: She Said "I'm Tired." I Built a Management System.
listen-before-giving-expertise.teaser: She says she is tired. He responds with schedules, charts and a mountain of binders. Once he finally listens, even his best advice learns to wait its turn.
paragraphs: The opening joke is visible before the advice even arrives. The woman in the loose green blouse is slumped at the desk with one hand against her head, a floral mug and laptop beside her, saying she is tired, cannot get anything done and feels mentally scattered. Across from her, the man in glasses and a white shirt is already typing. She has offered a description of how her day feels; he reacts as though she has handed him a project brief. That mismatch gives the first page its gentle comic tension.

His response then becomes wonderfully excessive. The laptop fills with a color-coded time-management chart, a sleep plan specifying Bed 23:00, Up 7:00 and 8 hours, plus an efficiency section listing Focus, Fewer distractions, Exercise and Daily review. In the next panel, the screen has effectively escaped into the room: huge stacks of binders labeled Time management, Sleep plan and Efficiency system rise across the desk until only the woman's eyes are visible behind them. The more complete the system becomes, the less space she seems to have.

The turning point comes when the woman finally says, "Actually... I just wanted to finish telling you about my day." The man stops and recognizes the mistake himself: he has been answering questions he imagined before listening to what she was actually saying. On the lower page, the change is concrete rather than abstract. He closes the laptop and asks, "Want me to listen first, or help find a solution?" She answers, "Let me finish first." In the next panel he pours tea into her floral mug instead of opening another spreadsheet.

Panel 09 shows what listening looks like in this story. The woman gestures as she explains that two meetings clashed and her lunch went cold; the lunch container is still sitting on the desk as a small, specific proof of the exhausting day she meant to describe. The man listens with his chin resting on his hand. A thought bubble marked "Efficiency plan" appears beside him, but a bold red X crosses it out. The joke is affectionate: the urge to optimize has not vanished, but this time he notices it and lets it pass without interrupting.

The ending shows that the story is not against advice; it changes the timing and permission around it. After the woman says the conversation helped, she later asks how to begin tomorrow's presentation. The man does not unload another system. He first asks, "Want one small tip?" Only after she says yes does he suggest, "Start with a specific example." His final thought—"Even knowledge has to take a number. No cutting in."—turns the lesson into a queueing joke. Read alongside the chapter line about knowing the masculine and keeping to the feminine, the comic can be seen as a contemporary reflection on holding capability without always pushing it forward: strength can include making room, receiving what another person is saying, and waiting until help is actually invited. That is one possible connection, not the only meaning of the ancient text.
listen-before-giving-expertise.quote: Know the masculine, keep to the feminine, and become the valley of the world.
listen-before-giving-expertise.practice: The next time someone says, "I'm tired," you might try one small question before offering a fix: "Do you want me to listen first, or help think through a solution?" If they choose listening, consider closing the laptop, setting the advice aside and letting them finish before deciding what comes next.
listen-before-giving-expertise.comicTitle: She Said "I'm Tired." I Built a Management System.
listen-before-giving-expertise.comicAlt: A twelve-panel Gongbi-style office comic follows a tired woman in green and a man in glasses and a white shirt. After she says she is exhausted, he creates detailed time-management, sleep and efficiency plans until a mountain of binders hides her. She explains that she only wanted to finish talking. He closes the laptop, asks whether she wants listening or solutions, pours tea and hears about clashing meetings and a cold lunch while mentally crossing out an "Efficiency plan." Later she asks for presentation advice; he first asks permission, then gives one small tip: start with a specific example. The closing joke says that even knowledge has to take a number and cannot cut in line.

help-without-taking-over.title: I Came to Help. Then I Took Over Your Life.
help-without-taking-over.teaser: He offered to help with a move. Soon he was choosing the furniture, the curtains and which memories to throw away. An old chair brings him back to his actual job: carrying the boxes.
paragraphs: The opening joke is how quickly a small offer of help expands into a complete takeover. The woman says, "I'm moving next week. A little nervous," and the man in orange workwear immediately answers with routes, van, packing, and everything else. In the next panels he is already pointing across a map marked "Old home" and "New home," presenting a coordinated furniture setup, and holding curtain samples. She is smiling throughout, so the humour comes not from hostility but from his cheerful efficiency gathering momentum faster than anyone asked it to.

The old wooden chair makes the boundary visible. While the surrounding furniture is clean and new, this chair is visibly worn, scratched, and personal. The woman touches it and says that although it is old, it means something to her. The man evaluates it as another logistical problem: too old, space-consuming, uncomfortable, ready to be removed. His reasoning is practical, but that is precisely the comic mismatch—he has become so committed to improving the move that he nearly optimizes away the one object whose value cannot be measured by neatness or convenience.

Panel 06 quietly changes the rhythm. The new room looks orderly, with coordinated curtains, furniture, plants, and moving boxes, yet the woman stands in the middle with her arms open and says, "Lovely... I just feel a bit unnecessary in it." The lower page does not answer this by producing another master plan. Instead, the man sits beside her with his tablet and asks, "So what, exactly, can I help with today?" That question is the turning point: the person receiving help now defines the job instead of being absorbed into somebody else's solution.

From there, the comedy becomes more physical and specific. She points to the heavy box labeled "BOOKS" and says she will choose the rest herself; he rolls up his sleeve and jokes that he is "Back to being the mover." They protect the battered chair together, and his "First class, then" turns the chair from unwanted clutter into an honoured passenger. In the curtain panel, she holds the fabric samples while he keeps the packing tape in his hand and says, "My advice can wait its turn." He is still useful and still funny, but his usefulness no longer requires control.

The final two panels make the change concrete rather than abstract. He carries the book box through the doorway while she positions her old chair where she wants it. Once the work is done, she sits comfortably on that same chair with a cup of tea, while he relaxes on the floor with a water bottle and says, "No life takeover today. Much lighter!" The closing line, "Help carry the boxes. Let them sign for their own life," connects the everyday joke with the supplied Daodejing excerpt as a contemporary reflection: effort can serve another person, but grasping their choices too tightly can defeat the purpose of helping.
help-without-taking-over.quote: Those who act upon it spoil it; those who grasp it lose it.
help-without-taking-over.practice: The next time you feel ready to organize everything for someone, you might first ask, "What, exactly, would you like help with?" Do the part they name, leave the remaining choices with them, and if another excellent suggestion appears, let it wait its turn.
help-without-taking-over.comicTitle: I Came to Help. Then I Took Over Your Life.
help-without-taking-over.comicAlt: Twelve-panel moving-day comic: a man in orange workwear enthusiastically plans a woman's route, furniture, and curtains, then nearly discards her worn old chair. After she says the perfect new home makes her feel unnecessary, he asks what help she actually wants. He carries her books, helps protect the chair, waits while she chooses curtains, and ends seated on the floor with a water bottle while she relaxes in her old chair with tea.

remove-one-extra-goal.title: My Plan Grew Three Kinds of Procrastination
remove-one-extra-goal.teaser: Her goals grow into a tree, but the first day ends without a single word of language practice. Removing one ambitious branch finally gives the others room to grow.
paragraphs: The opening turns an ordinary burst of motivation into a visual joke. The woman in blue announces, "Learn a language! Get fit! Start a channel! Finish my reading list! Starting today!" while her notebook repeats the four-item plan and the black cat watches from beside the desk. In the next panel, the plan has literally grown into a tree: "Language," "Fitness," "Channel," and "Reading list" hang among a clock, camera, books, globe, and other objects. Her delighted "Wow... My plan is growing! So motivating!" captures the funny moment when organizing a future self can already feel like progress.

Panels 03 and 04 show why that excitement becomes heavy. The woman tries to schedule exercise, video work, reading, and language into one packed day while eating at her laptop and handling her phone. Beside her, stacks labeled "Exercise log," "Video script," "Reading list," and "Language notes" rise like physical evidence of productivity. By night she is asleep across the desk next to the black cat, while a clock above the tree appears to melt downward. Her line, "A whole day gone... I still haven't spoken a word. So busy. Still not started," makes the central joke sharper: she has done a great deal around the goals without yet doing the small action she cared about most.

The turning point begins when the man in the red scarf does not offer another elaborate system. He looks at the crowded goal tree and says, "You hung every goal up there. Now you're stuck to the tree. Maybe trim one?" The woman first resists because she worries that choosing less will make her "less well-rounded." In Panel 06 she physically holds the "WELL-ROUNDED" card and asks whether she added it mainly to look impressive. On the lower page, that question becomes a decision: after the man suggests setting aside a goal that is mostly there for appearances, she reaches up and removes the "Channel" tag. The tree remains standing, and the other three goals remain visible.

The space created by that choice immediately becomes concrete rather than heroic. Wearing headphones, the woman speaks to the teacher on her laptop: "Hi! Nice to meet you! I'm nervous, but I finally spoke. Not as scary as I thought!" The teacher on screen answers, "Nice to meet you!" and her notebook records the modest achievement "Today: Spoke once." In the next panel she stretches beside the black cat while her checklist shows language practice and thirty minutes of exercise checked off, with the reading list still honestly marked "in progress." Nothing in the image suggests that she has mastered everything; the comedy and relief come from two real actions finally replacing a mountain of preparation.

The ending keeps the trade-off gentle rather than absolute. The man says that one less goal leaves more room for what she actually wants, and the woman replies, "Setting it aside wasn't failure. It made space for what matters." In the final panel she sits peacefully with a mug and the black cat beneath the tree, looking toward a bright city skyline. Only "Language," "Fitness," and "Reading list" remain hanging beside the softly distorted clock, and she says, "One less wish hanging on it. Now the tree can grow." The closing line, "Some wishes can wait. Let the ones that matter begin," connects naturally with Chapter 42's paradox of loss and gain without claiming that everyone should always pursue fewer goals; here, this particular character benefits from distinguishing what matters now from what can wait.
remove-one-extra-goal.quote: Some things are increased by being diminished; increased, they may instead be diminished.
remove-one-extra-goal.practice: Look at today's task list and notice whether one item is there mainly to make the plan look more complete rather than because it needs your attention now. Consider setting that one aside for ten minutes, then use the space for one small beginning you genuinely want: say one sentence in another language, take a short walk, or read one page with full attention.
remove-one-extra-goal.comicTitle: My Plan Grew Three Kinds of Procrastination
remove-one-extra-goal.comicAlt: A twelve-panel surreal comic follows a woman in blue whose four ambitions grow into a literal goal tree. After a packed day leaves her exhausted and still not speaking her target language, a man in a red scarf helps her question the "WELL-ROUNDED" goal. She removes the "Channel" tag, speaks "Hi! Nice to meet you!" to a teacher on her laptop, checks off language practice and thirty minutes of exercise, and ends beneath the tree with her black cat, a mug, three remaining goal cards, melting clocks, and a peaceful city skyline.
